title: The golden lion
hookLine: Fazang explains Huayan to the empress with a golden lion, and a room of mirrors

cards: A sutra so vast that an imperial court can't get hold of it. So the empress of China, who rules in her own name, asks a monk to explain it. Tradition says the monk doesn't open a book.
He points across the palace hall to a statue standing there, a lion made of gold, and begins to talk about it.
On another day, tradition says, he lines a room with mirrors facing one another on every side, sets a lamp and an image of the Buddha in the middle, and invites her in. Today, Fazang.

teach.b: First, the teacher. The monk is Fazang, a master of the Huayan school, named for the Flower Garland Sutra, and the empress is Wu Zetian. Second, the lion.

Fazang asks her to look at it two ways: the gold, which has no shape of its own, and the lion, the shape the gold has taken. Without gold there's no lion. Without some shape, the gold isn't anything you can see.
In his essay on the golden lion, the gold stands for the deep nature of things, and the lion for the world of particular things. They are not two.

teach.h: THE GOLD AND THE LION ARE NOT TWO.
teach.b: And since every part of the lion is gold, each single hair of the lion, the essay says, holds the whole lion. Third, the mirrors.
Stand in that room and the lamp appears in every mirror, and in every mirror's reflection of every other mirror, without end.
Huayan teaches that the world is like this: each thing reflects every other, and holds them all inside it.
The Flower Garland Sutra is linked with an image of the same idea, a net hung with jewels, each jewel shining with the light of all the rest. Fourth, why it matters on an ordinary day.

teach.h: NO ONE IS A SIDE CHARACTER.
teach.b: In Huayan's picture, if every thing contains every other thing, then no one is a side character.
The neighbor, the stranger on the stairs, the person you argued with: in this teaching, each one holds a reflection of the whole, and so does the one listening.

how: In Huayan and related traditions in China, Korea and Japan, students study the Flower Garland Sutra and Fazang's Essay on the Golden Lion, and teachers still use images like Indra's net and facing mirrors to explain how all things interpenetrate.

games.q: an empress asks you to explain a vast sutra her court can't follow. you're Fazang. what do you do?
o: point to the golden lion in the hall
tell her it is too deep to explain
games.why: Fazang used the golden statue: the gold and the lion's shape are not two, and every part holds the whole.

practice: If there's a window, a phone screen or a glass near you, look at how it holds the room; if not, close your eyes.
Bring one person to mind and notice who is reflected in them, who raised them, taught them, fed them, then notice yourself reflected there too, and let the reflections run on as far as they go.

wordCard.voice: Fazang. The Huayan master who showed the empress a golden lion to teach that the gold and its shape are not two, and that every part holds the whole. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese Huayan: flower garland, the name of the sutra and of Fazang's school.

carryVoice: Your line: mirrors in mirrors. In his picture, no one is a side character. Rest well; more tomorrow.
